question: In informal electronic waste recycling, how do documented worker and community exposure problems, academic studies measuring lead or other toxic exposures, and government/institutional collection or safety programs connect—and which interventions have measured outcomes rather than only proposed actions?

results.quote: Glazed ceramics, mining activities, improper e-waste management, and water and soil contamination emerged as the main exposure sources.
results.why: Systematic review synthesizing recent literature on early-life and reproductive lead exposure across Latin America and the Caribbean, identifying improper e-waste management alongside mining and ceramics as an exposure source linked to elevated blood lead levels and cognitive deficits.
results.limitations: Does not isolate or empirically measure informal e-waste recycling sites specifically, groups e-waste with multiple confounding exposure pathways, and does not evaluate any intervention or safety program.
results.source_identity_boundary: Publisher website and source citation do not independently establish truth or implementation.

results.why: Focuses on global public health threats from general microplastics, occupational inhalation in generic plastic industries, and the Global Plastics Treaty negotiations, with no discussion of informal e-waste recycling or electronic waste toxicants.
results.limitations: Does not address electronic waste recycling, heavy metals or plasticizers specific to e-waste, or e-waste intervention programs.
results.source_identity_boundary: Publisher website and source citation do not independently establish truth or implementation.

results.quote: This protocol provides a framework for evaluating the health status, metabolic indicators, and phthalate exposure among e-waste workers in Vietnam and supports occupational health evaluation.
results.why: Describes the methodology and initial cohort recruitment of a cross-sectional study protocol designed to quantify occupational phthalate plasticizer exposure and biomarkers among informal e-waste workers in Bui village, Vietnam.
results.limitations: Reports study design and preliminary demographic/PPE feasibility data only; it does not report finalized exposure-outcome associations, longitudinal causal effects, or evaluated safety interventions.
results.source_identity_boundary: Publisher website and source citation do not independently establish truth or implementation.

results.quote: The instrument provides a structured and context-specific tool for evaluating occupational safety culture, safety practices, and health effects within formal e-waste recovery facilities in Malaysia and may support future occupational health monitoring and intervention efforts.
results.why: Documents the psychometric development and factor validation of a safety and health questionnaire (E-WISE) designed to evaluate compliance and hazard perceptions among e-waste recovery workers.
results.limitations: Investigates formal licensed recovery facilities rather than informal e-waste settings, and validates a survey measurement tool rather than evaluating actual exposure reductions or program intervention outcomes.
results.source_identity_boundary: Publisher website and source citation do not independently establish truth or implementation.

results.why: Covers solar ultraviolet radiation hazards, stratospheric ozone recovery under the Montreal Protocol, and the launch of the SunSmart Global UV mobile application for sun protection.
results.limitations: Contains no content related to electronic waste, toxic metals, or recycling occupational health interventions.

results.why: Reports on the inter-agency expansion of the One Health partnership (FAO, WHO, WOAH, UNEP) and broad frameworks on antimicrobial resistance.
results.limitations: Does not address e-waste management, recycling worker hazards, or environmental toxicant biomonitoring.
results.source_identity_boundary: Publisher website and source citation do not independently establish truth or implementation.

results.quote: In 2019 only 17% of e-waste was documented as being properly collected and recycled. Exposure to improperly managed e-waste and its components can cause multiple adverse health and developmental impacts especially in young children.
results.why: Provides macro-level global background from a WHO compendium on municipal and hazardous solid waste, documenting the low rate of formal e-waste collection and identifying open burning and improper e-waste handling as causes of adverse community and worker health impacts.
results.limitations: Provides secondary aggregate global statistics without reporting primary local empirical biomonitoring data, specific informal site field observations, or measured intervention outcomes.
results.source_identity_boundary: Publisher website and source citation do not independently establish truth or implementation.

results.limitations: Concerns clinical and hospital waste streams and does not examine informal or formal electronic waste recycling, e-waste toxic exposures, or e-waste program outcomes.
